subtopic_detail: Perineal trauma reclassified on per rectum examination after an initial assessment of a second degree tear
stem:
You are the obstetrics and gynaecology registrar asked to review perineal trauma in the birth room. A 24-year-old woman in her first pregnancy gave birth twenty minutes ago by forceps for a prolonged second stage, with a right mediolateral episiotomy, and the baby weighed 4180 g.

The midwife has assessed the trauma as a second degree tear and has drawn up local anaesthetic to repair it in the room. The woman has an epidural in place that remains effective.

You examine her with good lighting and an assistant. The episiotomy extends through the perineal muscles towards the anal margin. On per rectum examination with the index finger in the anal canal and the thumb on the perineum, you can feel a defect in the external anal sphincter that involves more than half of its circumference. The anorectal mucosa is intact and the internal anal sphincter is felt to be continuous.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84/min, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9°C
data_table.Birth details: Forceps birth for prolonged second stage, right mediolateral episiotomy, birth weight 4180 g
data_table.Perineal examination: Episiotomy extending through the perineal muscles towards the anal margin
data_table.Per rectum examination: External anal sphincter defect involving more than half its circumference; internal anal sphincter continuous; anorectal mucosa intact

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Transfer her to theatre for repair of the sphincter under regional anaesthesia
options.rationale: A defect involving more than 50 per cent of the external anal sphincter with an intact internal sphincter is a 3b tear, and every obstetric anal sphincter injury is repaired in theatre with adequate anaesthesia, good lighting, appropriate instruments and an operator trained in the technique. Repair in these conditions materially reduces the rate of persisting faecal incontinence compared with repair attempted in the birth room. (Source: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears

options.text: Repair the perineal muscles in the birth room under local anaesthetic infiltration
options.rationale: This is the correct management of a genuine second degree tear, which by definition spares the anal sphincter complex. Repairing the muscle layer over an unrecognised sphincter defect is the commonest route to a persisting occult injury and later faecal urgency. (Source: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears

options.text: Leave the tear to heal by secondary intention and arrange physiotherapy review
options.rationale: Healing by secondary intention is an accepted option for superficial first degree tears and labial grazes that are haemostatic and well apposed. A divided sphincter will not reappose spontaneously and delayed secondary repair has substantially worse continence outcomes. (Source: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears

options.text: Repair the vaginal epithelium only and arrange colorectal review in six weeks
options.rationale: Deferring sphincter repair for six weeks allows retraction and fibrosis of the divided muscle ends, which makes secondary repair technically harder and functionally inferior. Primary repair at the time of birth is the standard of care. (Source: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears

options.text: Transfer her to theatre for a defunctioning colostomy and delayed sphincter repair
options.rationale: Faecal diversion is reserved for extensive cloacal-type injuries, gross faecal contamination or breakdown of a previous repair, and it is not required for a routine sphincter injury. Primary repair without diversion heals well in the great majority of cases. (Source: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears

explanation.summary: Obstetric anal sphincter injuries are graded as 3a when less than half the external sphincter thickness is torn, 3b when more than half is torn, 3c when the internal sphincter is also involved, and fourth degree when the anorectal mucosa is breached. The grading matters because it dictates the repair technique and predicts continence outcome, and it can only be determined by a per rectum examination, which is why that examination is recommended after every vaginal birth regardless of how the perineum looks. Risk factors include first vaginal birth, birth weight above 4 kg, occipito-posterior position, prolonged second stage, shoulder dystocia and instrumental birth, with forceps carrying a higher risk than vacuum. Repair is performed in theatre with a broad spectrum antibiotic, using either end-to-end or overlap technique for the external sphincter and end-to-end for the internal, with long-acting absorbable suture. Postnatal care includes laxatives for 10 to 14 days, physiotherapy, and a follow-up review at which the woman is counselled about mode of birth in a future pregnancy.
key_points: Grade 3a is under half the external sphincter, 3b over half, 3c includes the internal sphincter
Perform a per rectum examination after every vaginal birth to avoid missing an occult injury
Repair all sphincter injuries in theatre with adequate anaesthesia and a trained operator
Give a broad spectrum antibiotic and prescribe laxatives for 10 to 14 days afterwards
Forceps carries a higher sphincter injury risk than vacuum extraction
explanation.pearls: Avoid constipating agents and rectal examinations in the first days after repair, and prescribe lactulose rather than a bulking agent alone; a hard first stool passed against a fresh repair is a recognised cause of breakdown.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears
Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Perineal repair
BMJ Best Practice: Obstetric anal sphincter injury

subtopic_detail: Ascending motor block with bradycardia after an epidural top-up for caesarean section
stem:
You are the obstetrics and gynaecology registrar scrubbed for a category 2 caesarean section in a 31-year-old woman at 39 weeks. The anaesthetist topped up her labour epidural six minutes ago with 20 mL of lidocaine 2 per cent with adrenaline and is testing the block.

She first says both her hands have gone 'pins and needles', then that her arms feel heavy. Over the next two minutes her voice becomes weak and whispery and she tells you she cannot take a deep breath. She has not had a seizure and has described no metallic taste, tinnitus or perioral numbness at any point.

Her skin is warm and dry with no rash or wheeze. The block is now demonstrable to C6 bilaterally with absent grip strength. Her blood pressure has fallen from 124/76 to 68/34 mmHg and her pulse from 96 to 42/min. The uterus is displaced to the left and she is receiving 15 L/min oxygen by reservoir mask.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 42/min, blood pressure 68/34 mmHg, respiratory rate 8/min and shallow, SpO2 94 per cent on 15 L/min by reservoir mask, temperature 36.6°C, foetal heart rate 110/min
data_table.Block assessment: Sensory block demonstrable to C6 bilaterally with absent grip strength and a weak whispery voice
data_table.Skin and airway: Warm and dry, no rash, no wheeze, no stridor
data_table.Neurological features: No seizure, no metallic taste, no tinnitus, no perioral numbness
data_table.Drug given: Lidocaine 2 per cent with adrenaline, 20 mL via the epidural catheter six minutes ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Treat as anaphylaxis with intramuscular adrenaline 0.5 mg and a rapid fluid bolus
options.rationale: Anaphylaxis is the other cause of sudden profound hypotension in this setting, but it produces tachycardia with warm vasodilated shock accompanied by rash, wheeze or angio-oedema, and it does not produce a symmetrical ascending motor block. Bradycardia with a demonstrable C6 sensory level points to sympathetic blockade of the cardioaccelerator fibres instead. (Source: ANZCA: Management of high neuraxial block)
source_refs: ANZCA: Management of high neuraxial block

options.text: Give intravenous lipid emulsion 1.5 mL/kg for local anaesthetic systemic toxicity
options.rationale: Intravascular injection of local anaesthetic announces itself with perioral numbness, metallic taste, tinnitus, agitation and then seizures or ventricular arrhythmia, none of which has occurred here. Lipid emulsion treats that syndrome and does nothing for drug that has tracked into the wrong compartment intact. (Source: ANZCA: Management of high neuraxial block)
source_refs: ANZCA: Management of high neuraxial block

options.text: Sit her fully upright to limit cephalad spread and give high flow oxygen by mask
options.rationale: Sitting a woman upright once the sympathetic block is established removes venous return from an already vasodilated circulation and can precipitate cardiac arrest. Head-up positioning is used in the first minute or two of a hyperbaric spinal to limit spread, not as rescue for an established high block with hypotension. (Source: ANZCA: Management of high neuraxial block)
source_refs: ANZCA: Management of high neuraxial block

options.text: Give intravenous magnesium sulfate 4 g and prepare for immediate operative birth
options.rationale: Magnesium is given for eclamptic seizure prophylaxis, and she is normotensive by history with no proteinuria and no seizure. Magnesium would additionally worsen the hypotension and potentiate the neuromuscular weakness she already has. (Source: ANZCA: Management of high neuraxial block)
source_refs: ANZCA: Management of high neuraxial block

options.text: Intubate and ventilate her now and support the circulation with metaraminol
options.rationale: A block ascending to C6 with hand paraesthesia, loss of grip, a weak voice and shallow breathing is a high neuraxial block that has reached the phrenic and intercostal supply, so the airway is secured and ventilation taken over before respiratory arrest occurs. Bradycardia with hypotension reflects blockade of the T1 to T4 cardioaccelerator fibres and is treated with a vasopressor plus atropine, keeping left uterine displacement and preparing for immediate birth once she is stable. (Source: ANZCA: Management of high neuraxial block)
source_refs: ANZCA: Management of high neuraxial block

explanation.summary: High and total neuraxial block follows unintentionally extensive spread of local anaesthetic, most often when an epidural catheter has migrated intrathecally or subdurally and is then topped up with a surgical dose. The presentation is a recognisable sequence rather than a single sign: paraesthesia and weakness in the hands as the C6 to T1 roots are blocked, a weak whispery voice and difficulty breathing as intercostal and then phrenic function is lost, bradycardia from blockade of the cardioaccelerator fibres at T1 to T4, and profound hypotension from sympathectomy. It is distinguished from local anaesthetic systemic toxicity, which is a central nervous system excitation syndrome with no motor block, and from anaphylaxis, which produces tachycardia with cutaneous or airway signs. Management is airway first with intubation and ventilation, then circulation with vasopressors, atropine and fluids, maintaining left uterine displacement and proceeding to birth. The block wears off over one to three hours, so the woman needs continued sedation and ventilation until motor function returns.
key_points: Hand paraesthesia and loss of grip mark ascent of the block to the lower cervical roots
A weak voice with shallow breathing signals impending respiratory failure, so secure the airway early
Bradycardia with hypotension reflects blockade of the T1 to T4 cardioaccelerator fibres
Distinguish from local anaesthetic toxicity, which causes seizures without a motor block
Keep left uterine displacement throughout and continue ventilation until the block recedes
explanation.pearls: An epidural catheter that has previously worked normally can still migrate intrathecally, so a test dose is repeated before every top-up intended to produce a surgical block rather than only at insertion.

sources.label: ANZCA: Management of high neuraxial block
RANZCOG: Maternal collapse in pregnancy and the puerperium
BMJ Best Practice: Complications of neuraxial anaesthesia

subtopic_detail: Sequencing glucocorticoid and thyroid hormone replacement in postpartum hypopituitarism with hyponatraemia
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to the emergency department to see a 29-year-old woman who is five weeks postpartum. Her partner says she has been 'dragging herself around' for a month and has vomited repeatedly today and is now muddled about the date.

Her birth was complicated by a postpartum haemorrhage of about 4 litres from uterine atony, requiring eight units of red cells and a uterine balloon tamponade. She never produced any breast milk despite persistent attempts with a lactation consultant, and has had no vaginal bleeding of any kind since the lochia settled.

She is drowsy but rousable with sparse axillary hair. Investigations are shown. A computed tomography scan of the brain shows no haemorrhage, no mass and no hydrocephalus.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 58/min, blood pressure 84/50 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 35.9°C
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 121 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), glucose 2.8 mmol/L (3.5-7.7), creatinine 68 micromol/L (45-90)
data_table.Endocrine results: 9 am cortisol 42 nmol/L (200-650), free thyroxine 6.1 pmol/L (10-20), thyroid stimulating hormone 1.2 mIU/L (0.4-4.0)
data_table.Imaging: Computed tomography of the brain shows no haemorrhage, mass or hydrocephalus
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, sparse axillary hair

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Give intravenous levothyroxine now and start hydrocortisone in the morning
options.rationale: Thyroid hormone increases the metabolic clearance of cortisol, so replacing thyroxine in an unrecognised or untreated cortisol deficiency can precipitate an adrenal crisis. The sequence is fixed: glucocorticoid first, thyroid hormone second. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology

options.text: Give intravenous hydrocortisone now and add levothyroxine after twenty four hours
options.rationale: A low cortisol with hypoglycaemia, hypotension and hyponatraemia is secondary adrenal insufficiency, and glucocorticoid replacement corrects the blood pressure, the glucose and the sodium because cortisol deficiency is what is driving the inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion. Thyroxine is added once glucocorticoid replacement is established, since giving it first can precipitate an adrenal crisis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology

options.text: Give 3 per cent hypertonic saline 150 mL and restrict her fluid to a litre daily
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is reserved for hyponatraemia with seizures or deep coma, and correcting the sodium without correcting the cortisol treats the consequence rather than the cause. Fluid restriction is actively harmful here because she is hypotensive and volume depleted from vomiting. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology

options.text: Give intravenous desmopressin now and restrict her fluid intake to a litre daily
options.rationale: Desmopressin treats cranial diabetes insipidus, which produces hypernatraemia with large volumes of dilute urine, the opposite biochemical picture to this. Posterior pituitary function is usually preserved in postpartum pituitary necrosis because it has a separate blood supply. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology

options.text: Give oral tolvaptan now and restrict her fluid intake to one litre each day
options.rationale: Vasopressin receptor antagonists are used for euvolaemic hyponatraemia from the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion after adrenal insufficiency has been excluded. Using one in undiagnosed cortisol deficiency risks rapid overcorrection without addressing the hypotension or the hypoglycaemia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology

explanation.summary: Sheehan syndrome is ischaemic necrosis of the anterior pituitary following severe postpartum haemorrhage, and it occurs because the gland roughly doubles in size during pregnancy while remaining supplied by a low pressure portal system that is vulnerable to hypotension. Failure of lactation is usually the earliest clue because prolactin secreting cells are among the first lost, followed by amenorrhoea from gonadotrophin deficiency, then the insidious fatigue of secondary hypothyroidism and secondary adrenal insufficiency. The biochemical signature is a low target hormone with an inappropriately normal or low trophic hormone, so a free thyroxine of 6.1 pmol/L with a thyroid stimulating hormone of 1.2 mIU/L is diagnostic of central rather than primary hypothyroidism. Hyponatraemia in this setting comes from glucocorticoid deficiency releasing antidiuretic hormone from its normal cortisol mediated restraint, which is why it corrects with hydrocortisone rather than with saline. Presentation is often delayed by months or years, so the postpartum haemorrhage history must be actively sought in any woman of childbearing age with unexplained hypopituitarism.
key_points: Failure to lactate after a major postpartum haemorrhage is the earliest and most specific clue
Low free thyroxine with a normal thyroid stimulating hormone indicates central hypothyroidism
Hyponatraemia in cortisol deficiency corrects with glucocorticoid, not with saline or fluid restriction
Always give glucocorticoid before thyroxine, as thyroxine can precipitate an adrenal crisis
Posterior pituitary function is usually spared, so diabetes insipidus is uncommon
explanation.pearls: Take the cortisol and thyroid samples before the first hydrocortisone dose if it can be done within minutes, but never delay treatment for them: a random cortisol below 100 nmol/L in a shocked patient is diagnostic enough to act on.

subtopic_detail: First-line treatment for difficulty discarding possessions without obsessions or compulsive rituals
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 62-year-old woman referred by her general practitioner after a home visit. The practitioner's letter says the hallway and both bedrooms are filled chest-high with newspapers, plastic containers and unopened mail, and that the kitchen bench and the stove cannot be reached.

She tells you the items are 'all things I will need one day' and that the thought of putting any of them out makes her feel physically sick. She collects free newspapers and takes containers from recycling bins because she cannot bear to see them wasted. She has stopped inviting her sister in and eats takeaway because she cannot cook.

She describes no intrusive thoughts about contamination, harm or symmetry, and performs no checking, washing or counting rituals. Her mood is reactive, her appetite and sleep are unchanged, and she scores 28 out of 30 on the Montreal Cognitive Assessment. She holds no beliefs that the items have special powers.

data_table.Mental state: Reactive mood, no psychomotor change, no perceptual disturbance, insight that the accumulation is a problem
data_table.Obsessive compulsive features: No contamination, harm or symmetry obsessions; no checking, washing or counting rituals
data_table.Functional impact: Kitchen bench and stove unreachable; hallway and both bedrooms filled chest-high; social withdrawal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.text: Start high dose fluoxetine and review her response again in twelve weeks
options.rationale: Serotonin reuptake inhibitors at high dose are first line for obsessive compulsive disorder, where they act on the obsessions that drive the compulsions, and the evidence for them in hoarding disorder as a standalone condition is much weaker. Medication is added when a comorbid depressive or obsessive compulsive disorder is present or when therapy alone has not worked. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.text: Arrange a council clean-out of the property and review her again afterwards
options.rationale: Forced clearance without the person's participation reliably produces acute distress and rapid reaccumulation, because it removes the objects without changing the beliefs and decision-making difficulties that generated them. Enforced clearance is reserved for genuine public health or fire risk and is done alongside therapy, not instead of it. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.text: Start low dose risperidone and review her response again in twelve weeks
options.rationale: An antipsychotic would be considered if the beliefs about the possessions were held with delusional intensity, for instance that the objects were sentient or had special powers. She retains insight that the accumulation is a problem, which places this outside the psychotic spectrum. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.text: Refer her for cognitive behavioural therapy specifically adapted for hoarding
options.rationale: Difficulty discarding possessions with distress on parting from them and excessive acquisition, in the absence of obsessions and compulsive rituals, is hoarding disorder, and the treatment with the best evidence is a specifically adapted cognitive behavioural therapy. It targets the decision-making and categorisation difficulties, the beliefs about the objects, and the acquisition behaviour, typically with in-home sorting practice alongside clinic sessions. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.text: Refer her for neuropsychological testing and defer treatment until it is completed
options.rationale: Cognitive assessment matters when hoarding emerges for the first time in later life with other features of frontal or degenerative disease, and a Montreal Cognitive Assessment of 28 out of 30 argues against that. Deferring treatment for testing that is unlikely to change management wastes the therapeutic window. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

explanation.summary: Hoarding disorder was separated from obsessive compulsive disorder in DSM-5 because its phenomenology, course and treatment response differ. The defining features are persistent difficulty discarding possessions regardless of their value, distress associated with discarding, and consequent accumulation that congests living areas, with excessive acquisition present in most cases and specified when it occurs. The differential includes obsessive compulsive disorder where hoarding is driven by contamination or harm obsessions, a depressive episode with amotivation, psychosis with delusional beliefs about the objects, autism spectrum collecting, and frontotemporal dementia when onset is late and accompanied by other behavioural change. Insight is specified as good, poor or absent, and poor insight is common and does not exclude the diagnosis. Response to treatment is slower and less complete than in obsessive compulsive disorder, and the safety issues of fire risk, falls, vermin and structural load often need parallel attention from fire services and council.
key_points: Hoarding disorder requires difficulty discarding plus distress plus congestion of living areas
The absence of obsessions and rituals distinguishes it from obsessive compulsive disorder
Adapted cognitive behavioural therapy is first line; serotonergic medication has weaker evidence
Forced clearance without participation causes distress and rapid reaccumulation
New onset hoarding in later life warrants consideration of frontotemporal dementia
explanation.pearls: Animal hoarding is a distinct and more severe presentation, almost always accompanied by absent insight and squalor, and it carries much higher recidivism after intervention than object hoarding, so it warrants involvement of animal welfare services from the outset.

sources.label: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

subtopic_detail: Investigating excessive daytime sleepiness with episodic loss of muscle tone triggered by laughter
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 19-year-old university student referred with a query of depression. She says she has been falling asleep in lectures and once at the wheel at traffic lights, and that this has been going on for about eight months.

Her sleep diary shows she goes to bed at 11 pm, falls asleep within five minutes, and wakes at 8 am without an alarm. She takes a fifteen minute nap between classes and wakes from it 'completely refreshed for a few hours'.

She also describes that when she laughs hard her knees buckle and her jaw sags for a few seconds while she remains fully aware, and that two or three mornings a week she wakes unable to move for about a minute and sometimes sees a figure standing by the door as she falls asleep. Her mood is bright and reactive, she is engaged with her course and friends, she scores 3 on the Patient Health Questionnaire 9, and her body mass index is 22 kg/m2.

data_table.Sleep pattern: Bed 11 pm, sleep onset within 5 minutes, wakes 8 am without an alarm; refreshing 15 minute naps
data_table.Episodic features: Knee buckling and jaw sagging for seconds when laughing, with preserved awareness; sleep paralysis two to three mornings weekly; hypnagogic visual hallucinations
data_table.Mental state: Bright reactive mood, engaged with study and friends, Patient Health Questionnaire 9 score of 3
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 22 kg/m2, neurological examination within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor and review her again in six weeks
options.rationale: The hypersomnia of a depressive episode is unrefreshing, is accompanied by low mood, anhedonia and diurnal variation, and does not produce brief episodes of muscle weakness triggered by emotion. A Patient Health Questionnaire 9 score of 3 with a bright reactive mood makes depression an implausible explanation. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation: Narcolepsy)
source_refs: Sleep Health Foundation: Narcolepsy

options.text: Start modafinil now and arrange sleep studies only if she does not respond to it
options.rationale: Treating first and investigating later removes the ability to interpret the sleep studies, because stimulants alter sleep latency and suppress rapid eye movement sleep. Formal diagnosis is also required in Australia for subsidised access and for the driving and occupational advice that follows. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation: Narcolepsy)
source_refs: Sleep Health Foundation: Narcolepsy

options.text: Refer for overnight polysomnography followed by a multiple sleep latency test
options.rationale: Brief bilateral loss of muscle tone triggered by laughter with preserved consciousness is cataplexy, and combined with daytime sleepiness, sleep paralysis and hypnagogic hallucinations this is narcolepsy type 1. Diagnosis requires overnight polysomnography to exclude another cause of disrupted sleep followed immediately by a multiple sleep latency test, which shows a mean sleep latency of 8 minutes or less with two or more sleep onset rapid eye movement periods. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation: Narcolepsy)
source_refs: Sleep Health Foundation: Narcolepsy

options.text: Advise sleep hygiene measures and review her sleep diary again in six weeks
options.rationale: Insufficient sleep syndrome is the commonest cause of sleepiness in this age group and responds to extending sleep opportunity, but her diary already shows nine hours of consolidated sleep. Sleep hygiene advice is a useful adjunct in narcolepsy alongside scheduled naps, not a substitute for diagnosis. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation: Narcolepsy)
source_refs: Sleep Health Foundation: Narcolepsy

options.text: Arrange overnight oximetry and refer her for continuous positive airway pressure
options.rationale: Obstructive sleep apnoea produces unrefreshing sleep with snoring and witnessed apnoeas, typically in an older or higher weight patient, and naps are not restorative. A body mass index of 22 kg/m2 with refreshing short naps and cataplexy points elsewhere. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation: Narcolepsy)
source_refs: Sleep Health Foundation: Narcolepsy

explanation.summary: Narcolepsy type 1 results from loss of hypothalamic orexin producing neurons, probably through an autoimmune mechanism in genetically susceptible people, and it is defined by excessive daytime sleepiness plus cataplexy or a low cerebrospinal fluid orexin concentration. The classic tetrad of sleepiness, cataplexy, sleep paralysis and hypnagogic or hypnopompic hallucinations represents intrusion of rapid eye movement sleep phenomena into wakefulness, although fewer than a third of patients have all four. Cataplexy is the one feature that is close to pathognomonic and is distinguished from syncope and seizure by the emotional trigger, the preserved consciousness and the rapid complete recovery. Naps that are short and refreshing help separate it from the unrefreshing sleepiness of depression, sleep apnoea and insufficient sleep. Treatment combines scheduled naps and sleep hygiene with modafinil or another wake promoting agent for sleepiness, and venlafaxine or sodium oxybate for cataplexy, alongside mandatory discussion of driving and notification requirements.
key_points: Cataplexy is brief bilateral weakness triggered by emotion with consciousness fully preserved
Short refreshing naps separate narcolepsy from depressive and apnoeic hypersomnia
Diagnosis needs overnight polysomnography then a multiple sleep latency test
Diagnostic criteria are mean sleep latency of 8 minutes or less with two or more sleep onset rapid eye movement periods
Do not start a stimulant before the sleep studies, as it invalidates the result
explanation.pearls: Untreated narcolepsy with cataplexy makes a person unfit to drive in Australia; a conditional licence can be granted once treatment has produced satisfactory control, documented by a sleep physician, and the patient carries a legal obligation to notify the driver licensing authority.
